reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .368 xwOBA and .496 xSLG are doing something his batting average isn't — they're telling you his contact quality is elite even as he chases at 34.1% and strikes out 26.1% of the time. The gap between those damage numbers and a 64th-percentile xBA is the whole argument: he hits the ball hard enough to project 43 home runs, but the chase rate gives pitchers a lever, and if they find it consistently, the strikeouts compound into something uglier than the projection assumes. What saves the line is 11.6% walks and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, the latter in the 96th percentile, turning outs into singles and singles into stolen bases. If the chase rate stays where it is and pitchers attack him early in counts, you're looking at a solid regular rather than the near-MVP version this Statcast card is flirting with.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-four home runs in a full season is a serious number for a 23-year-old, and the Statcast profile says he's earned it: 93.0 mph average exit velocity and a 50.4% hard-hit rate place him among the most dangerous contact-makers at this level, and the .499 xSLG shows the power translating into expected damage rather than loud outs. The 11.8% walk rate pairs with an 18.2% strikeout rate to give him a contact-and-discipline floor that keeps the .280/.365/.538 projection grounded. The one real weight on the profile is that 1st-percentile OAA at third base, meaning his bat has to carry essentially everything, and a defensive move would reshape the conversation around his value entirely.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The .481 xSLG at 22 years old is the number that matters here, and the 13.5% barrel rate, sitting at the 89th percentile, is exactly why the projection's 36 home runs aren't a stretch. The gap between his xSLG and his hard-hit rate (38.9%, barely above the middle of the pack) tells you the power comes from contact quality and barrel frequency, not pure volume of loud contact, which makes it repeatable as long as he keeps getting to the barrel at that rate. The 27.0% whiff rate and 21.8% strikeout rate are the profile's hinge: if pitchers find a hole to exploit consistently, the xwOBA, currently .350, slides toward his xBA (.256), and what's left is a hitter who still profiles as a middle-of-the-order bat without the full force of a .265/.337/.486 line behind it.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .402 xwOBA and 2.72 xERA exist in the same body, which still hasn't stopped being remarkable. On the hitting side, the contact profile carries a real tension: a 15.9% barrel rate and 93.4 mph average exit velocity sit in a frame that also posts a 30.9% whiff rate, meaning he punishes mistakes at an elite level but can be put away, and the 13.2% walk rate is what keeps the .379 OBP honest when the bat misses. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball paired with 30.4% whiff rate and a contact profile that holds opponents to an 87.4 mph average exit velocity explains the xERA; the 7.6% walk rate is the one lever that could loosen the whole thing if it climbs. The projection of .279/.379/.534 with 37 home runs as a DH while returning to a rotation is only remarkable because we've stopped being surprised by it.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the swing-and-miss is a real problem, and that tension defines exactly what Jordan Walker is. A 92.4 mph average exit velocity with a 13.5% barrel rate puts him among the game's most dangerous pure hitters when he connects, and the .352 xwOBA says the underlying production is legitimate. But a 35.9% chase rate and 30.8% whiff rate are the load-bearing numbers on the other side — the projection's .282/.339/.488 across 672 PA is only available if pitchers can't exploit that zone management consistently enough to keep him off-balance. If the chase rate holds where it is, he's a .260-something hitter with 30 home runs and real value; if he tightens it even modestly, the power profile pushes him into a true middle-of-the-order bat.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the swing-and-miss is the price of admission. De La Cruz sits at 93.8 mph average exit velocity and a 13.7% barrel rate, both in the top tenth of the league, and the Statcast profile translates cleanly to the .360 xwOBA — the underlying quality of contact is exactly what you'd expect from those numbers. The problem is a 27.8% whiff rate that drags the K% to 27.2%, and that's the lever the whole profile turns on: if pitchers can keep expanding, they will. What keeps this from being a cautionary tale is that his 10.6% walk rate is meaningful enough to hold the floor, and 30 stolen bases in a projection of 638 PA adds a dimension that the slash line alone doesn't capture. The ValuCast projection of .269/.348/.477 with 25 home runs is what a genuine impact player looks like when he's also the most vulnerable hitter in the lineup, and right now, he's both.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact profile is the thing to watch, and right now it's fighting itself. Merrill's .467 xSLG and 46.4% hard-hit rate say real power, but his 37.4% chase rate drags the output back toward the middle — a 6.6% walk rate at 23 doesn't leave much margin for pitchers to exploit that aggressiveness before counts go sideways. The projection lands at .242/.294/.423 across 665 PA, which is basically what you get when elite contact quality runs into a below-average understanding of the zone: the slug is there, the on-base is thin. Add 27 projected steals and you have a player whose 29.0 ft/s sprint speed keeps him in the lineup conversation even when the bat underperforms, but the ceiling here hinges entirely on whether the chase rate bends as he matures.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

Bichette's .277 xBA sits in the 88th percentile, meaning the contact quality is genuinely there, but a 41.0% chase rate puts him in the bottom five percent of the league and suppresses everything downstream, keeping the xwOBA at a middling .323 and the walk rate at just 6.6%. The projection lands at .265/.313/.396, which is a second-division regular at shortstop: useful, not a difference-maker. If he ever stops expanding the zone, the bat sharpens fast; if he doesn't, 687 plate appearances of .709 OPS is what the Mets are getting.

reports.name: Nolan McLean
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate carries the argument here, but the walk rate is what keeps this from being a cleaner story. McLean punches out 26.7% of batters while a 27.8% chase rate, below-average for a pitcher with his strikeout production, tells you those punchouts are coming mostly in the zone, not by getting hitters to wave at air. The 9.5% walk rate is the dependency: if that number doesn't come down, the .293 xwOBA and 3.56 xERA represent his actual floor, not upside he's already banking. ValuCast projects 182.3 innings and a 3.13 ERA, which prices in some regression in the walks alongside continued contact suppression, and the contact numbers, a 6.3% barrel rate and 87.8 mph average exit velocity, suggest the quality-of-contact control is genuine enough to make that projection defensible.

But the underlying contact quality is the kind of thing that survives adjustments.

reports.name: Otto Lopez
reports.published_report: The .282 xBA sits in the 91st percentile, and the 13.0% strikeout rate matches it — Lopez makes contact at a rate very few hitters in the league can claim, and the projection's .301 AVG reflects exactly that. The exit velocity and barrel numbers are middling, which is why the .325 xwOBA lands only around the middle of the pack, but that's not the profile's engine. Thirty-three projected steals at 28.5 ft/s sprint speed, plus eligibility at both middle-infield spots, is what turns a bat-first contact hitter into a genuine everyday contributor. The 5.2% walk rate is the one real drag: if he can't get on base beyond what his hit tool earns him, the .339 OBP ceiling is probably the floor too, and the offensive value lives or dies on batting average holding.

reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: A 4.3% strikeout rate is essentially the entire argument. Arraez makes contact at a historically elite clip, his 7.8% whiff rate sits at the top of the game, and that .291 xBA reflects something real: he puts the ball in play constantly and knows exactly where to put it. The catch is that his 19.3% hard-hit rate and 1.2% barrel rate are about as soft as contact gets at the big-league level, so the projection's .315 AVG and .777 OPS depend entirely on him continuing to thread balls through gaps rather than elevate them, and a defensive shift in approach or a park that punishes soft grounders could shave a meaningful chunk off that average without giving him any power to fall back on.

reports.name: Charlie Condon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the anchor. At AAA in 2026, Condon has drawn 69 walks against 128 strikeouts across 520 plate appearances, and that 13% walk rate translates to 11.2% at the MLB level, well clear of the 8.5% the average big-league lineup produces. The .390 OBP at AAA is built on genuine plate discipline, not a BABIP mirage, and the .234 ISO shows real power behind it. The translation softens things honestly: his MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .177 and his strikeout rate ticks to 25.3%, a touch above the 22.0% MLB mark, so the ceiling here is a first baseman who gets on base and hits for moderate power, not a masher. If the strikeout rate doesn't compress against big-league arms, the floor is a bench bat who walks too much to cut, which is its own kind of useful, but the profile needs the power to stay close to the translation for him to hold down an everyday job.

Everyday middle-order regular; the walks give him a useful floor through a power dip. The sample covers 520 PA in Triple-A, so confidence is high.

reports.name: Parker Messick
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.91 and the xwOBA against is .266, both in the 91st percentile, and neither figure requires a fastball-velo excuse. At 94.3 mph, Messick isn't overpowering anyone; his barrel rate of 4.6% and hard-hit rate of 32.3% say he gets weak contact through shape and location, not velocity. The strikeout rate at 25.3% and walk rate at 6.8% are solid but not otherworldly, which means the whole profile hinges on whether he continues to suppress contact quality at this rate as hitters accumulate looks. If it holds, the projection of 189.5 innings, a 2.65 ERA, and a 1.06 WHIP looks like a genuine mid-rotation anchor; if the contact suppression erodes even modestly, there isn't a swing-and-miss ceiling to fall back on.

reports.name: Randy Arozarena
reports.published_report: The .344 xwOBA is doing a lot of the heavy lifting here, sitting well above a profile where the barrel rate is dead-average and the sprint speed has quietly slipped to 27.0 ft/s. Exit velocity backs the contact quality — 90.6 mph average with a 77th-percentile xwOBA says the batted-ball shape is genuinely better than the barrel number alone implies, but the stolen base projection of 24 depends on legs that the sprint speed data no longer obviously supports. What makes him work is the walk rate: 10.1% BB and a 21.6% K rate combine for the kind of on-base discipline that holds an OPS together even when the power isn't loud. If the speed decline continues and the contact quality softens toward that middling xSLG, you're left with a solid-average regular; if the discipline holds and Seattle keeps him in a lineup that protects him, the projected .812 OPS is the floor.

He's racked up 124 strikeouts against just 28 walks in 86 innings, and the command profile reads as genuinely advanced for a 22-year-old at this level. If the role holds, that strikeout-to-walk shape is exactly what a viable rotation piece looks like.

reports.name: Masyn Winn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile splits cleanly in two: elite plate discipline, no juice. Winn's 24.2% chase rate sits at the better end of the league, his strikeout and walk rates are right at the middle of the pack, and the contact itself is fine — a .248 xBA that lands exactly at the median. But a 3.6% barrel rate and 35.0% hard-hit rate are bottom-quartile power numbers, and the .333 xSLG confirms there's almost nothing to drive. The projection at .240/.315/.333 reflects that split honestly: a shortstop who won't beat himself, plays elite defense by OAA, and runs well at 28.4 ft/s, but whose offensive ceiling is constrained almost entirely by whether the bat-to-ball skills and speed can manufacture value that the raw contact quality won't. If the discipline holds and the legs age gracefully, he's a second-division regular who helps himself on the bases and never kills a lineup; if the power floor doesn't tick up at all as he matures, the profile slides toward a good-glove bench piece who starts against lefties.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the best thing about this profile, and it mostly holds the whole thing together. Rogers gets chases at a 34.5% clip, an 87th-percentile mark, but hitters don't whiff at 23.6% when they do swing, which is why the strikeout rate sits at a below-average 20.9%. He's a contact manager more than a swing-and-miss arm, and with 2475 rpm of fastball spin he can generate weak contact when his command keeps the ball in favorable counts. An xBA of .202 and a 28.7% strikeout rate tell the same story: Jensen makes hard contact when he connects, 91.1 mph average exit velocity and a 44.1% hard-hit rate are genuine, but he doesn't connect often enough for it to matter much. The .291 xwOBA is the ceiling of what the bat quality produces once the strikeouts take their cut, and a full-season projection of .224/.310/.410 with 22 home runs is essentially what you'd expect from a catcher who hits the ball hard in small windows between whiffs. The one thing that keeps him from being a total liability at the dish is an 11.1% walk rate, which gives him a floor; if that rate erodes as pitchers learn he'll chase in his spots despite the 23.9% overall chase rate, you're left with a defense-first roster piece whose bat is an afterthought.

reports.name: Zach Root
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates. Across AA & A+, 103 punchouts in 76.3 innings produces a 12.1 K/9, and the MLB-equivalent reads 9.0, which clears the 8.6 bar the average big-league arm clears. That's the good news, and it's genuinely good. The problem sitting right next to it is 36 walks in that same sample, a 4.2 BB/9 that translates to 4.3 while the typical MLB arm sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% that looks impressive at 21% against this prospect pool but lands right at the 13.5% MLB average once you run it through the translation. If the command sharpens, you have a setup arm. If it doesn't, the strikeouts keep him in a rotation conversation longer than he deserves, and you're settling for multi-inning bulk work.

reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The fastball is genuine, 96.9 mph with 2330 rpm of spin, and that's about where the good news peaks. A 44.4% hard-hit rate and an 89.8 mph average exit velocity tell you hitters are making loud contact, and a 22.3% whiff rate that sits in the bottom quarter of the league explains why: the stuff doesn't miss enough bats to outrun the damage. The xERA of 4.19 and a projected 4.62 ERA over 153.2 innings are consistent with each other, which is the kind of agreement that isn't a coincidence. If his command sharpens enough to turn that 8.2% walk rate into a weapon rather than a drain, there's a mid-rotation innings-eater somewhere in the profile; if it doesn't, he's a back-end starter burning through a Brewers rotation that needs more than that.

reports.name: Justin Crawford
reports.published_report: The speed is the profile. At 29.6 ft/s, Crawford runs at the 97th percentile, and the 19 projected steals in 476 plate appearances reflect that the tool is already translating. The problem is everything else in the Statcast card: a 1.3% barrel rate and .321 xSLG sit near the bottom of the league, the 37.2% chase rate undercuts a walk rate that's already modest at 6.3%, and an xwOBA of .286 says the contact quality isn't covering for any of it. What you're looking at is a gap-to-gap slap hitter who needs an exceptionally high contact rate to survive, and right now he's making contact that doesn't scare anyone. If the chase rate comes down and he learns to use the speed on the basepaths even more aggressively, there's a low-end everyday center fielder here; if it doesn't, he's a fourth outfielder whose legs keep him on a roster.

reports.name: Jacob Young
reports.published_report: Sprint speed at the 93rd percentile and a fielding OAA percentile at 98 make the whole case for Young, because the bat doesn't carry much weight on its own. His 31.5% hard-hit rate sits at the 16th percentile, and an xwOBA of .318 confirms the contact quality isn't quietly suppressed by bad luck. The strikeout discipline is legitimate, 16.7% K rate and 20.8% whiff rate both well above average, but a 7.0% walk rate near the bottom quarter of the league means he's not converting that plate control into on-base value. Project out 492 PA and you get a .248/.314 hitter with 20 stolen bases: a useful fourth outfielder who becomes a starting-caliber piece only if the speed and defense keep grading above what the bat deserves.

reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: The strikeouts and the contact quality live in completely different universes, and that gap explains everything about what Bradley is right now. His K% sits at 27.0 with a 97.1 mph fastball that grades out loud, but hitters are barreling him at 9.4% and making hard contact at 45.2%, both figures landing at the fifth percentile — meaning he gets whiffs, then gives back the damage on balls in play. The 10.0% walk rate is the compounding problem: without enough chase to compensate for the command lapses, the stuff plays smaller than the velocity suggests. If the control tightens and the contact profile regresses toward what a 27% strikeout arm should allow, the 3.85 xERA is a real ceiling; if it doesn't, the projection's 3.98 ERA over 174.6 innings feels like a best case.

Bolte hits the ball hard, 47.7% hard-hit rate, and runs like almost nobody in the sport at 30.5 ft/s, but when exit velocity and sprint speed don't translate into an xwOBA above .304, the swing-and-miss problem is the explanation. The projection's .341 OBP with 18 steals across 448 PA suggests a speed-first bench outfielder who can hurt you on the bases when he gets there, not a lineup fixture. If the strikeout rate ever softens, the tools behind it are real enough to push him toward everyday value; if it doesn't, he's a late-inning defensive sub and stolen-base threat off the bench.

Muñoz is whiffing 37.7% of hitters he faces with a 40.4% whiff rate, and both sit at the very top of the leaderboard; the 99.7 mph heater explains the swing-and-miss, and his 37.2% chase rate confirms hitters aren't just laying off. reports.name: Heriberto Hernández

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero
reports.published_report: The .447 OBP at A+ is the headline, and 83 walks against 96 strikeouts across 477 plate appearances is a real discipline profile for a 20-year-old center fielder. The 43 stolen bases add another layer — this is a player built around getting on base and creating damage with his legs. But the translation is where the argument gets complicated: the ISO drops from .185 at A+ to .133 at the MLB-equivalent level, and the MLB average sits at .150, meaning the on-base skills carry the whole thing and the power has to show up in more than gaps and speed. The ISO translates to .176, a notch above the MLB mean of .150, so there's real thump behind the patience. The real Bregman is a 23.3% chase rate and a 16.2% whiff rate, both elite by plate-discipline standards, meaning he earns his way on base by refusing to give away at-bats rather than by doing damage when he connects. The 86 strikeouts across 82.7 innings sound fine until you notice that a 9.4 K/9 in the minors translates to an 8.2 K/9 equivalent, a tick below MLB average, which means he's not missing enough bats to carry the profile on swing-and-miss alone. If the control holds, he's a depth arm who earns innings; if it slips, there's nothing else in the profile to absorb it.

reports.name: Edgardo Henriquez

The whole profile collapses into one problem: a 10.5% walk rate that sits well below average for command, and if he can't find the zone more consistently, all that swing-and-miss leverage gets diluted by free passes. reports.name: Austin Gordon
reports.published_report: The control-to-stuff gap is the whole argument here. At AA in 2026, Gordon has posted a 1.2 WHIP and 3.0 BB/9 across 115.7 innings, both sitting in the upper eighties percentile-wise among pitchers with meaningful volume, and his 39 walks in 24 starts reflect a pitcher who genuinely throws strikes. The problem is that the strikeouts don't match: 9.5 K/9 at AA translates to 8.0 against big-league hitters while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and his translated K-BB% of 12.8% trails the 13.5% MLB average. If the command holds but the swing-and-miss doesn't grow, this profile points toward the back of a bullpen rather than a rotation, a multi-inning or setup arm who keeps runners off base without overwhelming anyone.

reports.name: Robert Moore
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power split here is genuinely strange. Across 291 plate appearances at AAA in 2026, Robert Moore is hitting .227 with a .216 BABIP, yet his .239 ISO ranks in the 90th percentile of the hitter pool — 14 home runs with 41 strikeouts, which translates to an 18% strikeout rate when the MLB average sits at 22%. The walk rate translates to 8.9%, landing just above where the average big-league hitter checks in at 8.5%. The whole profile hinges on whether that BABIP normalizes upward; if it stays depressed, the .318 OBP won't move enough to make the power matter, and you're left with a bench bat who starts against lefties and doesn't hurt you. If contact finds him, the plus ISO with that strikeout shape is a real platoon piece.

reports.name: Caleb Bonemer
reports.published_report: The ISO is .312 across AA & A+, and that's the whole argument and the whole problem. Bonemer is 20 years old, slugging .562 with 35 home runs and 76 walks in 542 plate appearances, and the raw power translates to a .204 ISO equivalent at the MLB level — a figure that sits well clear of the .15 MLB average, framed differently than the gap usually gets framed because the gap is unusually wide. But the translation also puts his strikeout rate at 29.6%, and a .251 average backed by a .286 BABIP gives you no safety net if the contact doesn't tick up. If he finds enough contact to stay in the lineup every day, you're talking about a power-first everyday third baseman; if he doesn't, the 27% strikeout rate at this level becomes something worse against major-league pitching, and the floor is a bench bat who gets platooned out of the lineup before he gets a real look.

reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile has one loud number and one alarm. His fastball spin sits at 2537 rpm, which is genuinely elite territory, yet hitters are barreling him up at a 44.6% hard-hit rate and averaging 91.1 mph exit velocity off him — contact quality that lands near the bottom of the league. The spin isn't translating to swing-and-miss: a 22.3% whiff rate and 28.7% chase rate both sit well below average, which explains why the xERA lands at 4.49 despite the strikeout and walk rates being roughly league-typical. If he can learn to weaponize that spin into more deception, the projection's 4.20 ERA over 161.3 innings looks like a reasonable ceiling; if he can't, he's a back-end starter who gets hurt whenever his command slips even slightly.

reports.name: Scott Bandura
reports.published_report: The contact is legitimate — a 15% strikeout rate across AAA & AA that translates to 18.4% at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters post, backed by a .322 average in 556 plate appearances with only 86 strikeouts. Bandura also runs, 32 stolen bases this season, and gets on base at a .406 clip with 66 walks. The problem is the power: a .161 ISO in the minors translates to .133 in MLB context, below where you'd want it for a player without a carrying tool, and the ceiling here is honestly bench or platoon bat rather than everyday center fielder. If the speed and strike-zone discipline hold at the big-league level, he's a useful piece; if the bat-to-ball advantage shrinks even modestly, the light power leaves him short of a regular's value.

reports.name: Jacob Miller
reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. reports.name: Willson Contreras
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .374 and the xSLG is .483, and neither number is dragged down by contact quality — his 13.4% barrel rate is doing the work. The gap between those expected slugging marks and a .254 xBA tells you exactly what he is: a patient, pull-oriented masher who strikes out a lot and walks enough at 11.0% to make the strikeout rate tolerable, not pretty. The whole profile hinges on him continuing to barrel the ball at that rate into his mid-thirties, because if the barrel rate erodes, the strikeouts become the story instead of a footnote. If it holds, the projection of .270/.378/.506 with 30 home runs in 621 plate appearances is a legitimate middle-of-the-order catcher, which is rarer than people remember.

reports.name: Chad Patrick
reports.published_report: The 3.48 ERA projection is doing a lot of flattering work for a guy whose xERA sits at 4.08. Patrick's barrel suppression is the one genuine skill here, a 6.3% barrel rate that puts him in a range most middle relievers would envy, but his 21.2% strikeout rate and 9.5% walk rate leave almost no margin for contact to go wrong. The fastball at 95.5 mph has life that his whiff and chase numbers don't fully convert, which is the whole tension: if he can tighten the zone and squeeze a few more empty swings out of that velocity, the ERA projection isn't crazy; if the walk rate holds where it is, 4.08 is closer to the truth. A useful arm with a specific ceiling, probably a multi-inning bridge piece who makes a spot start when Milwaukee needs one, nothing more.

reports.name: Joey Cantillo
reports.published_report: The walk rate is what makes this profile difficult to trust. Cantillo generates whiffs at a 30.2% clip, which is genuinely loud, but an 11.9% walk rate drags the xERA to 3.96 and parks both his quality-contact metrics and his strikeout-to-walk relationship right near the middle of the league. The chase rate sitting at just 28.3% is the tell: hitters are getting themselves out in the zone rather than expanding off it, which means the whiff rate leans on location more than swing decisions, and location is exactly what's leaking. If the zone command never firms up, you're left with a back-end starter who needs 160.9 innings of defensive support to reach that 3.75 ERA, and that's a lot to ask of a guy whose margin for error is already thin.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Jadher Areinamo
reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
